To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

paternal autistic traits predict left frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) in infants with later symptoms of autism, but this is not true of maternal autistic traits, and that the effect of FAA on later symptoms of autism is stronger for girls than boys.
paternal but not maternal autistic traits predict frontal EEG alpha asymmetry in infants with later symptoms of autism, and that this association is stronger for girls than for boys.
paternal autistic traits, but not maternal autistic traits, predicted frontal alpha EEG asymmetry (FAA), which, in turn predicted child autism spectrum disorder symptoms in infants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of FAA in mediating the effect of parental autistic traits on child ASD symptoms.
the early markers of ASD in infants and their relation with parental autistic traits, with the aim to provide new insights into the etiopathogenesis of ASD.
the early detection of children who will develop an autism spectrum disorder (autism) and the identification of the underlying neurobiological processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
paternal autistic traits are associated to greater left FAA in infants, which in turn is associated to greater ASD symptoms in female infants.
the paternal autism phenotype is associated, in females, with greater left FAA and, in turn, with child ASD symptoms.
paternal but not maternal autistic traits predict frontal EEG alpha asymmetry in infants with later symptoms of autism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paternal autism phenotype is associated to child ASD symptoms, and that this pathway is mediated by FAA in infants.
paternal autistic traits, but not maternal ones, are associated with greater FAA which in turn, are associated with more child autistic traits.
the paternal autistic phenotype is associated with FAA in typically developing children and that FAA is associated with later child ASD symptoms, but only in female vs. male infants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
paternal but not maternal autistic traits are related to child ASD traits via FAA.
paternal but not maternal autistic traits predict child ASD traits through frontal asymmetry.
FAA is a potential early biomarker of ASD in female infants with a family history of ASD.
